ItemDifficulty.description:
How hard the professor *intended* an item to be.

Distinct from observed difficulty, which ``ainar score-items`` computes from
what the class actually did. Both are worth having precisely because they
disagree: an item declared ``easy`` that a third of the class fails is either
a badly worded question or a topic that did not land, and neither is visible
from the success rate alone.
ItemDifficulty.title: ItemDifficulty

ItemOption.description:
One answer option of a choice item.

A wrong option is more useful when it says *why* it is wrong. Mapping a
distractor to the concept it misreads turns "12 students chose (c)" into
"12 students are treating the validation split as unseen data", which is a
diagnosis rather than a score.

ItemRole.description:
Where an item sits relative to the task it belongs to.

``preparation`` is the one that carries behaviour rather than description. It
is asked *before* the work, to find out whether a student is ready, so a wrong
answer is an expected and useful outcome — ``ainar extract-evidence`` skips
these, because recording "did not demonstrate the concept" against a question
designed to be attempted cold would misread the whole point of asking it.

description:
One question or task inside an assessment.

A quiz scored only as a total tells you a student got 60%. The same quiz
with concept-tagged items tells you which concept cost them the other 40,
which is what concept states and gap detection actually need.
